items.title: Causes of the Revolt of 1857
items.body:
## A convergence of grievances

The Revolt of 1857 grew out of accumulated discontent across every section of society, usually grouped under five heads.

| Category | Key grievances |
|---|---|
| **Economic** | Deindustrialization; tariffs >80% on Indian textiles in Britain while British goods entered India duty-free; heavy land revenue impoverishing peasants; commercialization of agriculture (food to cash crops) |
| **Political** | Subsidiary Alliance, **Doctrine of Lapse** (Dalhousie) and direct annexation (e.g. **Awadh, 1856**) that stripped Indian rulers of power and prestige |
| **Administrative** | Corruption in police and judiciary; exclusion of Indians from higher posts; loss of patronage for artists and cultural figures |
| **Socio-religious** | **Religious Disabilities Act, 1850** (converts could inherit); reforms (Sati abolition 1829, Widow Remarriage Act 1856, female education) seen as intrusive; fear of forced conversion; racial discrimination |
| **Military** | **General Service Enlistment Act, 1856** (overseas service violating caste norms); lower pay and inferior treatment of Indian sepoys |

## The immediate spark

- The new **Enfield rifle** used cartridges rumoured to be greased with **cow and pig fat**; since the cartridge had to be bitten, it offended both **Hindus (cow)** and **Muslims (pig)**.
keyPoints: Five heads of causes: economic, political, administrative, socio-religious and military.
Political cause = Subsidiary Alliance, Doctrine of Lapse (Dalhousie) and annexations such as Awadh (1856).
Socio-religious = Religious Disabilities Act 1850 plus resented reforms (Sati abolition, Widow Remarriage Act 1856).
Military = General Service Enlistment Act 1856 requiring overseas service, plus unequal pay.
Immediate cause = greased Enfield cartridges offending Hindus (cow fat) and Muslims (pig fat).
items.mnemonic: Causes = 'PEAMS' shortcut: Political, Economic, Administrative, Military, Socio-religious.

items.title: Outbreak & Course of the Revolt
items.body:
## From Barrackpore to Delhi

- **Mangal Pandey** of the 34th Native Infantry attacked British officers at **Barrackpore** on **29 March 1857** (he was tried and **hanged on 8 April 1857**) — an early flashpoint.
- At **Meerut**, **85 sepoys** who refused the cartridges were court-martialled and jailed on 9 May; open rebellion broke out on **10 May 1857**.
- The Meerut sepoys marched to **Delhi** and proclaimed the Mughal emperor **Bahadur Shah Zafar (II)** the leader of the revolt, giving it a symbol of unity and legitimacy.

## Spread & civilian participation

- The revolt spread **from Punjab (north) to the Narmada (south)** and **from Bihar (east) to Rajputana (west)**.
- **Peasants, artisans, shopkeepers and zamindars** joined the sepoys, attacking law courts and revenue offices — symbols of British authority.
keyPoints: Mangal Pandey attacked officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857 (hanged 8 April 1857).
85 sepoys jailed at Meerut on 9 May; open revolt on 10 May 1857.
Meerut sepoys marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar the leader.
Spread from Punjab to the Narmada and from Bihar to Rajputana.
Peasants, artisans, shopkeepers and zamindars joined, attacking courts and revenue offices.

items.title: Major Centres, Leaders & British Commanders
items.body:
## Rebel centres and their leaders

| Centre | Rebel leader(s) |
|---|---|
| Delhi | Bahadur Shah Zafar, General **Bakht Khan** |
| Kanpur | **Nana Sahib**, Tatya Tope |
| Lucknow | **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, Birjis Qadir |
| Jhansi | **Rani Lakshmi Bai** |
| Bareilly | Khan Bahadur Khan |
| Faizabad | Maulvi Ahmadullah |
| Arrah (Bihar) | **Kunwar Singh**, Amar Singh |
| Baghpat | Shah Mal |

## British commanders who suppressed it

| Official | Role |
|---|---|
| Sir Colin Campbell | Commander-in-Chief; suppressed the revolt, relieved Lucknow |
| Sir Hugh Rose | Defeated Rani Lakshmi Bai |
| Henry Havelock | Key role in recapturing Kanpur |
| Colonel James Neill | Suppressed the revolt at Banaras |
keyPoints: Delhi — Bahadur Shah Zafar & Bakht Khan; Kanpur — Nana Sahib & Tatya Tope.
Lucknow — Begum Hazrat Mahal & Birjis Qadir; Jhansi — Rani Lakshmi Bai.
Bareilly — Khan Bahadur Khan; Faizabad — Maulvi Ahmadullah; Arrah — Kunwar Singh.
Sir Colin Campbell (C-in-C) and Sir Hugh Rose (defeated Rani Lakshmi Bai) led the suppression.
Henry Havelock recaptured Kanpur; James Neill suppressed Banaras.

items.title: Suppression & Reasons for Failure
items.body:
## Suppression

- **Delhi recaptured** on **20 September 1857**; Bahadur Shah Zafar was **exiled to Rangoon** and his sons executed.
- **Rani Lakshmi Bai** was killed in battle; **Tatya Tope** was captured and executed in **1859**.
- About **150,000 Indians**, including civilians, were killed.

## Why the revolt failed

- **Limited geographical spread** — mainly North India; the South, East and most of Western India (including Andhra) stayed calm.
- **No unified leadership, coordination or common ideology** — diverse, localised goals.
- **Superior British resources** — better arms and effective use of the **telegraph**.
- **Loyal Indian states** — Scindia of Gwalior, Holkar of Indore, the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Sikh rulers backed the British.
- **Class and social divisions** — many zamindars supported the British and educated Indians saw the revolt as backward-looking.
keyPoints: Delhi recaptured on 20 September 1857; Bahadur Shah Zafar exiled to Rangoon.
Rani Lakshmi Bai killed in battle; Tatya Tope executed in 1859; ~150,000 Indians killed.
Failure factors: limited spread, no unified leadership, superior British arms and telegraph.
Loyal states — Gwalior (Scindia), Indore (Holkar), Hyderabad (Nizam) and Sikh rulers helped the British.
Class divisions — many zamindars and educated Indians stayed aloof.

items.title: Consequences — Act of 1858, Proclamation & Army Reform
items.body:
## End of Company rule

- The **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred control from the **East India Company to the British Crown**.
- It created the **Secretary of State for India** — a member of the British Cabinet, accountable to Parliament and aided by a **Council of 15**.
- The **Governor-General** was additionally styled **Viceroy** (the Crown's representative); **Canning** became the first Viceroy.

## Queen's Proclamation, 1858

- Promised **non-interference in religious matters**, **equal opportunity** in appointments (not fully implemented), and recognition of **princes' rights** with an **end to annexations**.

## Reorganization of the army (Peel Commission)

- Raised the **ratio of British to Indian soldiers**; **segregated units by caste, community and region** to prevent unity; **excluded Indians from the artillery**; diversified recruitment toward Sikhs and Gurkhas.

## Wider impact

- Rise of **nationalism** and adoption of the policy of **'divide and rule'**; abroad, a policy of **'masterly inactivity'**.
keyPoints: GoI Act 1858 ended Company rule, transferring India to the British Crown.
Created the Secretary of State for India (Cabinet member, aided by a Council); Canning = first Viceroy.
Queen's Proclamation 1858 promised non-interference in religion and an end to annexations.
Peel Commission raised the British:Indian troop ratio, segregated units and barred Indians from artillery.
Aftermath: rise of nationalism, 'divide and rule', and 'masterly inactivity' abroad.

items.title: Administrative Structure After 1857
items.body:
## Indian Councils Act, 1861

- Added an **Imperial Legislative Council** to the Governor-General's council for **law-making**.
- The Governor-General nominated **6-12 additional members**, at least half **non-official** (Indian or English), usually princes, big zamindars, merchants or retired officials.
- It was **purely consultative** — no budgetary power, no right to question the executive; a bill needed the Governor-General's assent and could be **disallowed by the Secretary of State**.

## Provincial administration

- India was divided into provinces; the three **Presidencies (Bengal, Madras, Bombay)** under Governors had more powers; other provinces were run by **Lieutenant Governors / Chief Commissioners**.

## Decentralization of finance

| Viceroy | Reform |
|---|---|
| **Lord Mayo (1870)** | First separated central and provincial finances via **fixed grants** for police, jails, education, roads |
| **Lord Lytton (1877)** | Transferred more heads — **land revenue, excise, general administration, law & justice** |
| **Lord Ripon (1882)** | Divided revenues into **general, provincial and shared**, with a **five-yearly review** |
keyPoints: Indian Councils Act 1861 created the Imperial Legislative Council for law-making.
Members were nominated (6-12, half non-official); the Council was purely consultative with no budgetary power.
A bill needed the Governor-General's assent and could be disallowed by the Secretary of State.
Financial decentralization: Mayo (1870) fixed grants; Lytton (1877) more heads; Ripon (1882) shared revenues.
Three Presidencies (Bengal, Madras, Bombay) had more powers than other provinces.

items.title: Tribal, Peasant & Civil Uprisings (before & after 1857)
items.body:
## Why they matter for the exam

Before and after 1857, numerous **localised tribal, peasant and civil revolts** challenged Company/British rule. Prelims frequently pairs these with 1857 (terms like 'Ulgulan', leaders and dates).

| Revolt | Year(s) | Region / community | Leader(s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sanyasi Rebellion** | 1770s–1820s | Bengal | ascetics/peasants (cf. *Anandmath*) |
| **Kol Uprising** | 1831–32 | Chotanagpur | Buddho Bhagat |
| **Santhal Hul** | 1855–56 | Rajmahal hills (Bengal-Bihar) | **Sidhu & Kanhu** Murmu |
| **Indigo Revolt** | 1859–60 | Bengal | Digambar & Bishnu Biswas |
| **Munda Ulgulan ('Great Tumult')** | 1899–1900 | Chotanagpur | **Birsa Munda** |
| **Mappila (Moplah) revolts** | 19th c.–1921 | Malabar | Mappila peasants |

## Key exam hooks

- **'Ulgulan' = Birsa Munda's Munda rebellion (1899–1900)** for a *Munda Raj*; Birsa is honoured on **Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 Nov)**.
- After the **Santhal Uprising (1855–56)** the British created the **Santhal Parganas** and made it illegal for a Santhal to transfer land to a non-Santhal.
- The **Indigo Revolt** and later cultivation decline were driven by the ryots' resistance and by **synthetic (aniline) dyes** making natural indigo unprofitable by the early 20th century; *Neel Darpan* (Dinabandhu Mitra, 1860) dramatised planter oppression.
- V.D. **Savarkar** called 1857 the **'First War of Indian Independence'**; the British called it a 'Sepoy Mutiny'.
keyPoints: 'Ulgulan' (Great Tumult) = Birsa Munda's Munda rebellion, 1899–1900 (Chotanagpur); Janjatiya Gaurav Divas = 15 Nov.
Santhal Hul (1855–56) led by Sidhu & Kanhu; afterwards British created the Santhal Parganas with a land-transfer ban.
Kol Uprising (1831–32, Chotanagpur); Sanyasi Rebellion (Bengal, late 18th c.).
Indigo Revolt (1859–60, Bengal); indigo declined by early 20th c. as synthetic dyes made it unprofitable.
Savarkar termed 1857 the 'First War of Indian Independence'; British called it a Sepoy Mutiny.
items.mnemonic: Ulgulan = Birsa Munda (1899); Hul = Santhal (1855, Sidhu-Kanhu).
